OneKey Neo - An Honest Verdict and Review for $179

An honest review of OneKey Neo for $179 - an AMOLED screen, 2 EAL6+ chips, and 5 hidden downsides that marketing actually conceals

Official website

What is OneKey Neo?

The OneKey Neo wallet is a non-custodial open-source hardware crypto wallet for offline coin storage, equipped with 2 EAL6+ security chips, a 3.54-inch AMOLED screen, and Clear Signing transaction verification based on safeOS 2.

Neo is essentially a lite version of the Pro 2. The size is the same, the board is the same, the processor is the same… The only difference inside is the number of secure chips1

If you strip away the marketing chaff, OneKey Neo is the first budget wallet that feels not like a cheap plastic whistle or an archaic USB stick, but like a modern consumer-electronics gadget.

Quick assessment

My conclusion after testing is that the manufacturer made a smart move. Instead of cutting screen quality or slowing down the interface, OneKey took the platform of its flagship Pro 2 and removed the secondary toys from it - the fingerprint scanner, the QR-code camera, and the Apple Find My ecosystem.

Functionally, the wallet is rich. It is essentially a touchscreen mini smartphone with clear transaction signing and wireless charging.

At the end, for $179 you get 90% of the flagship’s real capabilities.

OneKey Neo Review

Hardware and ergonomics

In appearance and in-hand feel, Neo leaves a pleasant impression, and in three respects it even beats the flagship.

  1. Fiberglass is better than glass. The back panel of Neo is matte composite fiberglass. In my opinion, this is more practical than the glass back of the Pro 2. It doesn’t collect fingerprints and doesn’t risk cracking on the first drop onto tile.
  2. Large screen. The 3.54-inch AMOLED touchscreen with 60 Hz and 800 nits makes interaction smooth. You no longer hide the wallet in a safe for six months. The device turns into an aesthetic everyday work device for daily portfolio monitoring and signing dApp transactions.
  3. Grip nuance. Because of the rectangular edges of the aluminum frame without rounded corners, holding the device with two hands is less convenient than the rounded Pro 2. But at 51 grams, it doesn’t cause discomfort.

Security analysis

On protection, OneKey Neo maintains a reasonable balance. Here Maxim Anisimov, a well-known editor at bytwork.com, tore down the OneKey Neo and looked inside. The teardown of OneKey Neo showed that the motherboard is identical to the Pro 2 and carries a dual-core STM32H747XIH6 with a 50–60 fps interface.

On the board there are 2 isolated THD89 chips with EAL6+ instead of 4 in the Pro 2; one stores private keys and signs transactions, the second verifies the PIN code and system keys. There is a 700 mAh battery with Qi and AEC-Q100 components. The body is anodized aluminum, a 3.54-inch AMOLED under Gorilla Glass 5, IP56 protection.

And although dropping some functions will be debated:

  • 2 EAL6+ chips instead of 4. The teardown shows that Neo has 2 banking THD89 chips. In my opinion, resistance to hacking does not drop at all because of this. 2 chips fully cover key generation and PIN isolation. The extra pair of chips in the Pro 2 was needed only for biometrics and the camera.
  • Loss of Air-Gap (camera). Without a camera, autonomous signing via QR codes is impossible. For paranoids, that’s a minus. But for 95% of owners, the combination of Bluetooth, USB-C, and NFC is enough. It is a comfortable balance while preserving hardware isolation of keys.
  • Clear Signing. This is what really carries Neo’s security. And no, not the chips, but the readability of the screen. When you see the full decompiled transaction text and addresses without endless scrolling, the issue of blind signing is closed completely.

5 weak spots and pitfalls

I won’t pretend the device is ideal. Neo has plenty of downsides. There are 6 of them.

  1. An empty box for $179. The kit includes only the wallet and a cable. The silicone case, the $39 NFC SeedCard, and metal plates have to be bought separately.
  2. Slow update over Bluetooth. Over-the-air firmware can drag on for 30–40 minutes and fray your nerves if the connection drops. Update strictly via cable through a PC.
  3. Ignoring Bitcoin orthodox users. At launch there is no clean Bitcoin-Only firmware and no Sparrow Wallet integration.
  4. Hidden costs for SignGuard. The app’s full anti-phishing functionality (deep contract analysis) requires a paid subscription at $29.99/month.
  5. Unlock by PIN only. Without a fingerprint, you have to constantly enter the PIN on the screen, and this increases the risk of shoulder-surfing in public places.
  6. Finally, dependence on the app.

Also, the interface is strange in places, and a popular mistake is to choose the Import mnemonic option directly in the OneKey mobile app. And there is a software hot wallet function there. The keys end up on a networked device, and cold storage is completely nullified.

In addition, full anti-phishing protection and transaction simulation ask for a subscription of $29.99 per month or $239 per year. For Bitcoin, the service is almost useless - it is tailored to smart contracts in EVM networks.

Remember that the wallet isolates keys in an EAL6+ chip, but it will not save you from signing malicious permissions or from seed leakage due to improper storage.

Comparison of OneKey Neo with Ledger, Trezor, and Tangem

Below is a comparison of the OneKey Neo hardware crypto wallet with popular alternatives from Ledger, Trezor, and Tangem.

The comparison layout is as follows. In OneKey Neo, what immediately stands out is the bright touchscreen AMOLED display (3.54 inches, 60 Hz, 800 nits). Navigation is smooth, and 42-character addresses are read clearly. With E-ink (for example, in Ledger Flex), the refresh rate is noticeably lower and there is no color. Trezor’s display is noticeably smaller, and Tangem has no screen at all.

Quick start and setup of OneKey Neo

Check:

  1. Check the box and device
  2. Inspect the protective seals on the box and the tamper-evident sticker on the device itself.
  3. If the sticker is peeled off or the word VOID has appeared on it, do not activate the wallet and immediately contact official support.

Initial setup:

  1. Press and hold the side power button to turn on OneKey Neo.
  2. Choose the interface language. Russian is among the available options.
  3. Choose Manual Setup. This way private keys are generated completely offline, without the network and the app.
  4. Set a name for the device.
  5. Set and confirm a strong PIN code for daily access.

Seed phrase security:

  1. Tap Create Wallet.
  2. By default you will be offered 12 words. Through the 3-dot menu in the upper-right corner of the screen, you can choose 18 or 24 words (BIP-39) or SLIP-39 (Shamir Backup of 20 words).
  3. Write down the words strictly in order on the paper card from the kit or stamp them on a metal plate. Never photograph the phrase or enter it on the internet.
  4. Complete the verification of the written-down words on the device screen.

Next, connect the device to the app:

  1. Download the OneKey App only from the official website onekey.so.
  2. Connect OneKey Neo to a PC or smartphone via USB-C or Bluetooth.
  3. The app will automatically perform a cryptographic authenticity check of the chips and firmware (Genuine Check).
  4. Update the OS to the current version.

Update via a PC with a USB-C cable. It will take 2–3 minutes instead of 15–40 minutes over Bluetooth and will protect you from connection failures.

Final verdict. Who should buy it and who should skip it

My verdict. OneKey Neo is the best purchase in the sub-$200 segment for active Web3 users, DeFi traders, and those looking for a neat first cold wallet.

  • Buy Neo if you need a bright screen, fast contract signing, and reliable storage without overpaying $120 for biometrics and a camera.
  • Skip it if you are a Bitcoin maximalist and accept only physical Air-Gap via QR code, Bitcoin-Only firmware, and operation through Sparrow Wallet.

Balance of pros and cons

Strengths:

  1. Contract readability is top-notch, and the interface is fast - 60 FPS.
  2. FIDO2 Passkey is available - a physical USB key for Google, GitHub, and exchanges.
  3. Universal interfaces - USB-C, Bluetooth, NFC plus Qi wireless charging (IP56).

Weak spots:

  1. No camera (QR Air-Gap). The device cannot do autonomous signing by scanning QR codes - connection is only via Bluetooth, USB-C, or NFC.
  2. No fingerprint scanner and no Find My. Unlock is PIN-only, and Apple geolocation has been removed.
  3. Device Only package. The $179 box does not include the NFC SeedCard or a case - buy them separately.
  4. Bitcoin software is limited. At launch there is no Bitcoin-Only firmware and no support for third-party software (Sparrow Wallet) for multisig schemes.
  5. Updates are slow. safeOS 2 over Bluetooth takes from 10 to 40 minutes - in my experience, it is better to update only via USB-C cable (2–3 min).
